name: Freya Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government. We do not sell or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal day at work like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and still learning the delivery claims desk at a contact centre. I take afternoon calls, check tracking photos, and ask the lead to look over cases that might need a refund; I use AI search now and then, but I don't trust a neat answer without the record. I like putting a lost parcel right, and I hate closing the screen while wondering if the customer will have to ring again. Secondary school is my last qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team the little AI search box helps sometimes, but a customer still needs us to sort a missing parcel. I'd ask the shift lead to keep showing us how to check an answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI now and then, mostly to find an old reply, but I am still slow at the rest of the call system. My pay is low, the mortgage eats most of it, and we have less than a month of expenses saved. A quiet AI year isn't a quiet year at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the afternoon calls and ask the lead to check my delivery claims before I close them. Through the first year of this plateau, I'd put the school lunch money in an envelope first and stop buying café coffee on shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit relieved about the job, but I still count the days until payday. The small tool is not what keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which claim do you need help with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A customer had a parcel marked delivered while the photo showed the wrong doorway. I nearly closed it, but my lead showed me how to reopen the courier ticket before I answered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner think about the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Tomas works mornings, and we go over the bills together on Sundays. Our two children are school age; we protect their lunches before the small treats for either of us.

S0.quote: A quiet AI year isn't a quiet year at home.
say: I would say the **search box** can help, but agents still resolve missing parcels.
I would ask the lead for **answer checks** as I learn the call system.
think: I use AI sometimes, yet I am still **slow** with other call screens.
I have **less than a month** saved, low pay, and a mortgage that keeps me tense.
do: Keep taking **afternoon calls** and checking delivery claims with the lead.
Set aside **school lunch money** before other spending.
feel: **Relieved** about work, still watchful until payday.
fieldNote: Freya’s example of a **wrong doorway photo** shows she is still learning the claims process.
The household puts **school lunches** before small adult treats, even without major AI change.

steps.text: Keep handling afternoon delivery calls and check claims with the lead
Stop buying café coffee and put school lunch money aside first

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should try the new reply system on old cases before putting it in front of customers. I'd ask the staff group to insist on paid practice time for junior agents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Many of my calls are routine questions, and AI could take them before I have mastered the difficult ones. I could learn the new tool if someone showed me properly, but a shorter rota would reach our mortgage quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the experienced agent to show me three test cases each week and write down where the AI reply is wrong. I'd take those notes with coworkers to the staff group; in the first year after rollout, if my shifts fall, I'd ask the lender about a temporary payment arrangement and look at posted jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but I can put my hands on a task. I would rather practise now than wait for the first wrong customer refund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you bring to the staff group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the three examples with customer names removed and ask for paid time to check replies. It matters that the new agents get that time too, not just the people who already know the tricky cases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask the lender before applying elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply as well, but there are few centres nearby and an offer could take weeks. The mortgage date comes first, so I would rather ask for an arrangement before a payment is late.

S1.quote: The mortgage date comes first, so I would rather ask for an arrangement before a payment is late.
say: I would try **old cases** before sending AI replies to customers.
I would ask our **staff group** for paid practice time for junior agents.
think: I fear AI could take **routine calls** before I master the harder ones.
I could learn with help, but **shorter shifts** would hit our mortgage quickly.
do: Practise three **AI test cases** each week with an experienced agent.
Take anonymised **error notes** with coworkers to the staff group.
Ask the **lender** for an arrangement and apply for posted work if hours fall.
fieldNote: Freya proposes **three weekly cases**, making practice possible beside ordinary shifts.
She links a **group request** for paid time to a household plan before any mortgage payment is missed.

steps.text: Practise three AI reply cases each week with an experienced agent
Bring anonymised error notes with coworkers to the staff group
Ask the lender for a payment arrangement if shifts fall
Apply for posted local work if shifts fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the centre to put job dates and training pay in writing. I'd ask the staff group to make sure part-time and new agents are in the room when those promises are made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 could answer even the awkward delivery calls better and cheaper than I can. The robots are later, around 2031, but I sit at a screen; that delay does not pay this mortgage. We have less than a month of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for written notice with the staff group now and cancel the summer trip we were planning for the children. In the first year after AGI arrives, if my job ends, I'd apply for advertised paid kitchen assistant shifts at the school and ask my sister for help with one mortgage payment if wages do not arrive in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel sick thinking about telling the children the trip is off. I can make calls and fill forms. There is almost no buffer between a lost wage and the next bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the school kitchen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I helped serve lunch there at a community event, and I know the early shift fits our family better than late calls. I would ask if a paid vacancy exists; food preparation is hands-on, but robots around 2031 could change that work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we are staying close to home this summer because money is tight, and that it is the adults' problem to solve. I would not ask the children to reassure me.

S2.quote: There is almost no buffer between a lost wage and the next bill.
say: I would ask for **written dates** and training pay before jobs change.
I would include **part-time and new agents** in the staff group talks.
think: I expect AGI could take even my **awkward delivery calls** by 2028.
I know **2031 robots** do not delay screen-work losses, while our savings are below one month.
do: Ask for **written notice** with the staff group now.
Cancel the children’s **summer trip** to protect mortgage money.
Apply for advertised **paid school kitchen** shifts and ask my sister for one payment if wages are late.
feel: **Sick with worry** about the children and the next bill.
fieldNote: Freya chooses **school kitchen work** for its hours, while recognising robots might reach it around 2031.
Her plan for **one family payment** is a bridge, not a lasting source of income.

steps.text: Ask for written notice with the staff group before cuts
Cancel the planned children’s summer trip to protect mortgage money
Apply for advertised paid school kitchen shifts if the centre job ends
Ask her sister for one mortgage payment if wages are late

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years means the centre can give junior agents real practice instead of a course link sent at the end. I'd ask the staff group for paid sessions on the difficult calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn the harder claims and build a little savings before 2031, though AGI may still do those claims. School kitchen work would stay hands-on until around 2034, but I need a real paid opening, not a volunteer memory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask the lead for weekly claim practice and put a small amount into a mortgage envelope if full shifts hold. If the school posts a paid kitchen vacancy, I'd ask for a trial shift before applying; in the first year after AGI arrives, if my centre hours end, I'd apply for that job only if the pay and hours cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is still scary, but there is time to find out what a kitchen week pays. I can be careful without standing still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would paid practice change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn while still bringing home a wage, and the senior agents would have time to explain a mistake. I cannot pay for a long course out of a cupboard with almost no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a kitchen course first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the school said the course was required for a posted paid place and the fees were covered. I would try a paid shift first if one was offered.

S3.quote: I cannot pay for a long course out of a cupboard with almost no savings.
say: I would demand **paid sessions** on difficult calls before junior shifts disappear.
I would say five years permits **real practice**, not a last-minute course link.
think: I could improve claims skills and save a little before **2031 AGI**.
I need a **paid kitchen vacancy** before treating hands-on work as a bridge to 2034.
do: Ask the lead for **weekly claim practice** this year.
Fill a small **mortgage envelope** if full shifts hold.
Request a **paid kitchen trial** only if a vacancy is posted, then apply if wages cover bills.
feel: **Scared**, but able to check pay before changing work.
fieldNote: Freya sees paid practice as a way to **learn while earning**, not a guarantee against AGI.
She refuses a long course without **covered fees** and a posted paid vacancy.

steps.text: Practise difficult delivery claims weekly with the lead
Put a small amount into a mortgage envelope if shifts hold
Request a paid kitchen trial for a posted vacancy and apply if wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for the centre to teach junior agents properly and tell us each year what jobs are changing. I'd ask the staff group to keep the rota figures in view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 my children will be older, but I may still owe on the house. I can learn the call system and save more over a decade; AGI reaches screen work in 2036, while robots for hands-on work arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the afternoon calls and take paid practice on difficult claims if offered. Each month with full shifts I'd add a little to the mortgage envelope; in the first year after AGI arrives, if my job ends, I'd apply for a posted school kitchen place with enough hours and ask my sister about short help only if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less rushed, not safe forever. Our mortgage comes due every month, even in the ten years before AGI arrives in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change jobs before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a school offered steady paid hours that covered our bills, I would consider it. I would not leave the current wage for a short unpaid trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the staff group to count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How many junior shifts go, how many people get paid practice, and how many are hired into the new roles. A chart of faster calls alone would hide the part that matters to families.

S4.quote: Our mortgage comes due every month, even in the ten years before AGI arrives in 2036.
say: I would ask for **yearly job counts** and proper training for junior agents.
I would ask our **staff group** to track changes to the rota.
think: I could learn more and save over a decade, while the **mortgage** may still be due in 2036.
I know **2039 robots** follow AGI by three years; calls change first.
do: Keep **afternoon calls** and take paid claim practice if offered.
Add to a **mortgage envelope** each month that full shifts hold.
Apply for a posted **school kitchen** place if call work ends and pay covers bills.
feel: **Less rushed**, yet aware of monthly mortgage pressure.
fieldNote: Freya defines progress through **junior shifts** and **paid practice**, not faster call charts alone.
She would consider kitchen work earlier only for **steady paid hours** that cover the household bills.

steps.text: Keep taking afternoon calls and paid claims practice if offered
Add to the mortgage envelope in months with full shifts
Apply for a posted paid school kitchen place if centre work ends and wages cover bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Our mortgage needs both wages, and we have less than a month saved while I am still learning the desk. Written notice, paid practice, and a real opening with hours that cover bills would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who helps the new agents when a customer challenges a machine answer. Customers need somebody who can reopen a disputed delivery claim, not another screen saying the claim is closed.

headlineQuote: Customers need somebody who can reopen a disputed delivery claim, not another screen saying the claim is closed.
portrait: Freya is a **43-year-old junior agent** learning delivery claims after secondary school, using AI search only now and then.
She has **low pay**, less than a month saved, a partner, two school-age children, a mortgage, and few nearby centre jobs.
She prefers **tested tools** and paid practice, bringing error examples to the staff group with coworkers.
The **2028 AGI** date threatens both wages and the children’s summer plans; longer runways allow careful paid job trials.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her wages while the family has less than one month saved against a mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, paid practice, and a posted job with hours that cover household bills would help her move.
